The "Lando Norris effect" on your brain page — full explanation

1. What the Lando site actually does (the thing we're copying)

The Lando Norris homepage is not a 3D model of his head. It's a flat 2D photograph being manipulated by a shader so it behaves like 3D. That's the key insight, and it's exactly what makes it achievable for you.

The trick has two halves:

Half A — the helmet reveal. A second image (the helmet) sits layered over the face. As your cursor moves, a soft organic blob — not a hard circle — masks the helmet on/off. The colors "part" around your cursor like you're wiping fog off glass. The video transcript confirms it: a custom shader generates fluid blobs that follow cursor speed and direction, and those blobs decide which parts of the second image show through.

Half B — the depth illusion. The face image has a hidden companion: a depth map (grayscale image, white = near like the nose, black = far). The shader reads this depth map and pushes pixels around slightly based on cursor position. Near pixels shift more, far pixels shift less. Your brain interprets that differential shift as parallax — the face feels like it has real volume even though it's a flat photo.

That's the whole magic. Two flat images + one grayscale depth map + one shader.

2. How we're adapting it for your brain page

The Lando site reveals a helmet over a face. We invert the relationship and change the metaphor.

Lando
Your brain page

The metaphor matters. Your whole site is "the brain is a black box of infinite potential." The chromatic head is the black box — alien, iridescent, unreadable. When the visitor hovers, they part the chromatic surface and find Jayon, the actual person, underneath. Open the head, see who's inside. That's the entire site concept compressed into one gesture.

So on the Lando site the helmet is the "costume." On yours the chromatic dispersion is the costume, and the reveal is the truth.

3. The two behaviors, precisely

Your design-system.md locks two distinct cursor behaviors. Don't conflate them — they trigger in different zones.

Behavior 1 — Ambient depth parallax (whole page)

Active whenever the cursor is anywhere on the page. The chromatic head subtly shifts its pixels using the depth map. Spec value: maximum 0.02 UV offset.

That number is deliberately tiny. "UV offset" means how far we slide the texture sample point across the image — 0.02 is 2% of the image width at the absolute extreme. The point is restraint. Lando's site is famous for not being a wobbly gimmick; the parallax is so subtle you feel it before you consciously see it. We're matching that discipline. If it looks like the head is "swimming," we've gone too far.

Behavior 2 — The spotlight reveal (head silhouette only)

Active only when the cursor is inside the head's actual silhouette — not the bounding box, the real outline. This is what the alpha mask is for: a black-and-white image where white = head, black = everything else. The shader checks "is the cursor over a white pixel?" before triggering anything.

When the cursor is over the head:

A soft circular spotlight (~120px radius, ~40px feathered edge) follows the cursor

Inside that spotlight, the chromatic head fades down in opacity

The real face image shows through in the gap

The spotlight edge is feathered with noise — so it's not a clean circle wipe, it's chromatic colors breaking apart and parting, exactly like Lando's fluid blobs

The revealed face gets slight desaturation + faint chromatic aberration on its edges, so it doesn't look pasted in — it stays in the same visual universe as the chromatic shell

When the cursor leaves the silhouette, the spotlight fades and the chromatic head returns fully.

4. The technical stack — how it's built in code (Phase 2)

This is a Three.js plane with a custom GLSL fragment shader. Not a 3D model. One flat rectangle, one shader, four texture inputs:

A single PlaneGeometry, MeshShaderMaterial, with 4 textures:

  head_diffuse  →  the chromatic head (what shows by default)
  face_real     →  Jayon's real face  (revealed in the spotlight)
  head_depth    →  grayscale depth     (drives the parallax offset)
  head_alpha    →  silhouette mask     (defines where hover is "valid")

The fragment shader runs once per pixel, every frame, and does roughly this logic:

Read depth at this pixel → calculate a small UV shift based on cursor position → that's the parallax (capped at 0.02).

Sample head_diffuse at the shifted UV → the chromatic color for this pixel.

Check distance from this pixel to the cursor. Add a noise value so the boundary is ragged, not circular.

If the pixel is inside the noisy spotlight radius → blend in face_real instead, proportional to how deep inside it is.

Multiply everything by head_alpha → so the background never gets touched, only the head.

The shader gets two uniforms (live values JavaScript feeds in every frame): uMouse (cursor position) and uTime (for animating the noise so the edges shimmer slightly even when the cursor is still).

The depth map and alpha mask you generate from Depth Anything V2 on Hugging Face — that's an external-tool sub-step, flagged in the handoff doc as needed before Brain Page Step 6. We already have head_depth.webp; head_alpha.webp still needs generating.

5. The three tiers — and why we're locked to Tier 2

The handoff doc commits us explicitly:

Tier 1 — plain image swap on hover (instant, no shader). Ugly, but our fallback if the shader fights us.

Tier 2 — depth parallax + noise-feathered spotlight mask. ~1 day. This is V1. It captures ~90% of the Lando feel: the depth illusion and the organic reveal both land.

Tier 3 — full fluid chromatic dispersion shader where the chromatic effect itself is generated live and flows like liquid. 3–5 days. Post-V1 upgrade.

The difference between Tier 2 and Tier 3: in Tier 2 the chromatic look is baked into the head_diffuse image — it's a static photo of an already-chromatic head. In Tier 3 the chromatic dispersion is computed in real time and flows with the cursor. Tier 2 is the smart call because the visual payoff is nearly identical and the cost is a fifth of the time.

6. The honest gap between Lando and us

Two things to keep realistic:

The Lando reveal blob is genuinely fluid — it stretches and trails based on cursor velocity. Our Tier 2 spotlight is a circle with a noisy edge. It will read as organic, but it won't trail. That trailing behavior is Tier 3 territory. For V1, accept the noisy circle — it's the 90% version.
